To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) furosemide added to a combination of valsartan and rampril reduced proteinuria in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD); and that (2) the effect was partly explained by the reduction of estimated glomerular ﬁltration rate (eGFR).

the addition of furosemide to a combination of ramipril and valsartan was associated with a greater reduction in proteinuria than the combination of ramipral and valsartan alone, but that it was not associated with a greater decrease in the estimated glomerular function rate (eGFR) and was associated with more symptomatic hypoten- sive episodes.

the antiprotienuric effects of furosemide were not mediated by a decrease in estimated GFR and that the antiproteinnuric effect of furosemidewas greater with a lower dose of ramipri than with a higher dose.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of diuretics in combination with angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker.
the role of protein excretion in the progression of kidney disease and the effect of antihypertensive therapy on proteinuria.
the effects of RAAS blockade on the renal function of patients with chronic renal failure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the combination of RAAS blockers with diuretics can reduce proteinuria but the long-term renal outcomes remain to be elucidated.
diuretics may be added to RAAS blockers for patients with renal diseases who are not adequately controlled by RAAS blockers alone.
the addition of a diuretic to a RAAS blocker can decrease proteinuria in a selected group of patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
proteinuria reduction may not be a good surrogate marker for renal protection in the long-term.
proteinuria itself cannot serve as a marker of improved renal outcomes.
proteinuria is not an ideal outcome measure in renal diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the antiproteuric effect of furosemide in patients with diabetic nephropathy is partly due to a reduction in the estimated glomerular ﬁltration rate (eGFR) and that the combination of furosemidewith a RAAS blocker is associated with a higher incidence of symptomatic hypotension.

the combination of a diuretic with an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) or an angiotensins converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor is not recommended in the management of patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and proteinuria.
the antiprotienuric effect of furosemide is independent of its effect on renal haemodynamics.
